newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto says PPP will contest Pakistan election.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto says PPP will contest Pakistan election.

text.p: Ousted Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto said on Thursday her party would contest a general election called for February 3 and she asked the caretaker government to refrain from any witchhunts.
"We will have a full-scale participation in the elections," she told Reuters in an interview outside Karachi's Landhi Jail, where she met her detained husband, Asif Ali Zardari, for two hours.
Those who had been detained from her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) had been freed on bail, she said.
"The party has therefore decided not to boycott the elections and instead to participate in the elections," she said. "We still demand that there should be no political witchhunt."

President Farooq Leghari dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) and dismissed Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule. A caretaker government was appointed to hold fresh elections.
Bhutto has gone to the Supreme Court with a petition seeking a restoration of the 217-seat National Assembly and her government.

She said on Thursday that previously there was an impression that the PPP could not make a vigorous start to its election campaign because of uncertainty surrounding the elections and because of her petition now before the Supreme Court.
But she said the party had embarked on a fully fledged campaign because any court verdict was unlikely much before the election day.
Zardari had made a motion in court saying that, if any case had been registered against him, the authorities should at least tell him about it, but so far he had not been so informed, she said.

Zardari was first detained on November 5 under the catch-all Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance. He was re-arrested on December 19 on suspicion of involvement in the alleged murder Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza after a court declared his six-week detention illegal.

Zardari, who was investment minister in Bhutto's cabinet, denies any involvement in the killing of Murtaza in a police shootout in Karachi in September and he has accused the caretaker government of falsely implicating him.

Murtaza's Lebanese-born widow, Ghinwa, now chief of a breakaway faction of the PPP, has accused Zardari, former interior minister Naseerullah Babar, former Sindh province chief minister Abdullah Shah and police of conspiring the September 20 killing of her husband.
Police say Murtaza was killed in a crossfire after his bodyguards fired first at police.
A judicial tribunal is inquiring into the incident, which Benazir says was a conspiracy against her family and government.
Zardari has been at the centre of corruption allegations associated with Bhutto's government. Both deny any wrongdoing.
Bhutto said if her government were restored by the Supreme Court, she would expect President Leghari to function within the limits of Pakistan's constitution.
"I was elected by the people of Pakistan and not by one man, but I have been dismissed by one man and not the people of Pakistan," she said.
